title: Neighborhood price prediction: walk-forward test of leading signals against simple baselines
method_doc: docs/PREDICTION-MODEL.md (method fixed and committed before any evaluation)
question: Within a county, which tracts will see more house-price growth than the county's median tract over the next 5 (and 3) years?

decision.rule: The model is used for a county only if, pooled over test windows, its top-minus-bottom-fifth spread beats both the cheapest-tracts and the prior-trend baselines with 90% county-bootstrap intervals above zero, and in that county's own test cells it is not below either baseline.
decision.what_ships: the relative-value screen (cheap for its county) in every county, with its tested 5-year ranges by home-value fifth and its hit rate

headline: The leading-signal model did not beat the plain 'cheapest tracts' screen: over the next 5 years its top fifth of tracts beat its bottom fifth by 6.6 points (90% 5.2 to 7.9), against 6.4 for the cheapest-tracts screen; the difference, 0.2 points (90% -0.3 to 0.6), is not distinguishable from zero.
It did beat the prior-trend baseline, by 5.7 points (90% 4.1 to 7.2).
Without the price-level inputs the model's spread falls to 2.7 points: most of the edge is cheap tracts catching up.
The cheapest fifth's median 5-year gain over its county's median tract shrank from 10.6 points (windows starting 2015) to 2.4 (starting 2020).
So every county keeps the relative-value screen, now with its tested ranges and hit rate.
tested_on: tested on 48 counties, 5-year windows starting 2019 and 2020 (fitted only on earlier, non-overlapping windows); 3-year windows starting 2017-2022
units: points = 100 x log change relative to the county's median tract (close to percentage points for these sizes); hit rate = share of the tracts called 'top third' that ended in the county's top third (no skill = 0.333)

errors_from: training fit's own errors (no inner walk-forward fold)

baseline_fifth_ranges.note: points = 100 x log change vs the county median tract; [p10, median, p90, tracts]; fifth 1 = cheapest fifth by Census home value; added after the pre-registration (doc A.10)

caveats: Relative to the county: a county-wide rise or fall is not predicted.
FHFA's tract index is re-estimated every release, so the past values used here are today's revised figures, not what was known then; the same holds for LODES 2010-2021.
Only two 5-year test windows (starting 2019 and 2020) could be scored without overlapping the fitting windows; both contain the 2020-2022 boom.
After 2020 FHFA publishes fewer tracts (thin sales), so recent outcomes rest on the better-traded tracts.
The cheap-tracts edge shrank in recent windows: its 3-year top-minus-bottom spread was 13.29 points for windows starting 2017 and -1.44 for windows starting 2022; past catch-up may not repeat.
Tested on tracts; block groups get their tract's figures, labelled as tract-level.
The stated 80% ranges were too narrow in the test: the model's held 73% of 5-year outcomes and the screen's fifth ranges 73%, so outcomes spread wider than the range says.
Nothing here covers rents, cash flow or a price fall across the whole county.
